blocks.x: Core definitions

Amine A nitrogen-containing organic compound — an organic derivative of ammonia (NH3), formed when one, two or all three of ammonia's hydrogens are replaced by aliphatic, aromatic or cyclic organic groups. The N–H bonds of ammonia become N–C bonds in amines.
Ammonia (NH3) Note: ammonia itself is an inorganic compound, not an amine. It is basic in nature and acts as a nucleophile; its nitrogen atom is trivalent and sp3 hybridized.

Nucleophile vs. electrophile Two key species in organic chemistry: the nucleophile ("nucleus-loving", electron-rich) and the electrophile ("electron-loving", electron-poor). Amines are nucleophiles by virtue of the lone pair on nitrogen.
NH₃ (ammonia)→ 1° amine (R–NH₂)→ 2° amine (R₂NH)→ 3° amine (R₃N)
Each arrow represents the replacement of one more N–H hydrogen of ammonia by an organic (R) group.

blocks.x: 1° / 2° / 3° · symmetry · heterocyclic
One, two or all three of ammonia's hydrogens can be replaced by organic groups — aliphatic, aromatic, cyclic, or otherwise — and this substitution pattern is the basis for classifying every amine.
Primary, secondary & tertiary amines
Primary (1°)
Only one of the H's surrounding N is replaced by an organic group. General form: R–NH2.
Secondary (2°)
Two of the H's are replaced. General form: R2NH.
Tertiary (3°)
All three H's are replaced. General form: R3N.
Symmetrical vs. unsymmetrical amines

Applies only to 2° and 3° amines This classification is usually associated with secondary and tertiary amines, but not primary amines (which have only one organic substituent, so symmetry doesn't apply).
Symmetrical
All organic groups attached to N are identical, e.g. R2NH or R3N where every R is the same.
Unsymmetrical
The organic groups attached to N are different from one another, e.g. R(R')NH or R(R')(R'')N.
Aliphatic, aromatic & heterocyclic amines

blocks.title: Heterocyclic amines — neither aliphatic, aromatic, nor simply cyclic

blocks.x: A classroom exercise asks students to classify two compounds as aliphatic, aromatic or cyclic — the answer is none of the above: both are heterocyclic amines.
Heterocyclic compound: a cyclic compound in which the ring contains more than one kind of atom. In addition to carbon, one or more atoms of O, N or S may be present in the ring.

Heterocyclic compounds are described as important because they are intimately connected with the processes of life — examples include thiamine, folic acid, nucleic acids, haemoglobin and chlorophyll (see the Reactions & Importance tab).

blocks.x: Alkylamines · arylamines · IUPAC rules
Amines are named according to which type of group the nitrogen is attached to, and the amine functional group defers in naming priority to several other functional groups.
Alkylamines vs. arylamines
Alkylamines
Nitrogen atom is attached to an alkyl group (a saturated, chain or ring, carbon substituent).
Arylamines
Nitrogen atom is attached to an aryl group (an aromatic ring substituent).
Two IUPAC naming styles
Style 1 — analogous to alcohols: replace the "–e" ending of the corresponding alkane name with "–anamine".
Style 2 — substitutive: name the alkyl group and attach "–amine" as a suffix.
Amines and other functional groups

Lower naming priority The amine functional group is considered of lower priority when it occurs together with other functional groups such as –OH, –COOH, C=O. In such cases, the amine is named as an "amino–" prefix, while the higher-priority group determines the parent name and suffix.
Worked example: HOCH2CH2NH2 is named 2-aminoethanol — the parent is "ethanol" (from the –OH group), with "amino" as a substituent prefix, since –OH outranks –NH2.
Naming diamines

c: 1,4-Benzenediamine (two –NH<sub>2</sub> groups on the ring, at C-1 and C-4)

blocks.x: The "di–" prefix plus locant numbers indicates how many –NH<sub>2</sub> groups are present, and exactly where they sit on the parent chain or ring.

blocks.x: pKa · pKb · drug absorption

Amines are generally weakly basic (Lewis bases) in solution. How basic a given amine is — and how that basicity interacts with body pH — strongly shapes how amine-containing drugs are absorbed and distributed.
NH₃, a 1°, a 2° and a 3° amine
NH₃pKa 9.26
1° aminepKa 10.66
2° aminepKa 10.73
3° aminepKa 9.81
Bars scaled to pK<sub>a</sub>: the higher the pK<sub>a</sub>, the stronger the base — and the least positive pK<sub>b</sub> marks the strongest base.
Reading pKb / pKa Stronger bases have the least positive pKb values. Weaker bases have lower pKa values — equivalently, the higher the pKa, the stronger the base.
Order of basicity (aqueous solution) For simple alkylamines: 2° > 1° > 3°. (The lecture leaves the underlying steric/solvation reasoning for this trend as a self-study assignment.)

blocks.title: Why acid–base chemistry matters for drug absorption

items: The majority of drugs used in medical science exist as either acids, bases, salts, or are amphoteric in nature.
A drug's acid–base properties can greatly influence its bio-distribution and partition characteristics.
Most drugs (weak acids or weak bases) react with water to yield ionized species; the extent of ionization is determined by the pKa of the drug and the pH of the medium.
A drug molecule may exist in ionized form, unionized form, or an equilibrium mixture of both, depending on the pH of the body compartment it is in.
The ionized form penetrates cell membranes with difficulty (low lipid solubility); the unionized form, being lipid-soluble, diffuses through cell membranes with ease.
Weakly basic drugs with pKa values generally above 7.4 are absorbed well in the small intestine (pH 6–8), because there they exist mostly in the unionized, lipid-soluble form.

blocks.x: Nucleophilic chemistry · medicine · biology
Amines act as nucleophiles throughout their important organic chemistry, and nitrogen-containing heterocycles are woven into the core molecules of life.
Amines (nucleophiles) meet three common electrophiles

c: Carboxylic acid derivatives — especially acid chlorides or anhydrides

blocks.x: In each case, the amine's nitrogen lone pair is the nucleophile; only the identity of the electrophilic partner — and the resulting mechanism — changes.
Amines as products of nucleophilic reactions

Because amines are themselves formed and consumed as nucleophiles, the same three reaction families above (substitution at alkyl halides, addition to carbonyls, and acyl substitution at acid derivatives) underlie the standard routes used to prepare amines and to build them into larger, more complex nitrogen-containing molecules, including drugs.
Amines as pharmaceutical agents

Why this matters One of the lecture's stated learning objectives is to be able to identify amine drugs: the –NH2, –NHR or –NR2 group appears throughout medicinal chemistry, and a drug's amine functionality is often exactly what determines its acidity/basicity, its ionization behavior at different body pH values (see the Basicity tab), and therefore its absorption and distribution in the body.
Nitrogen heterocycles connected with the processes of life
THIAMINEA heterocyclic, nitrogen-containing vitamin (vitamin B<sub>1</sub>) cited by the lecture as an example of a biologically important heterocyclic compound.
FOLIC ACIDA heterocyclic compound essential to life processes, listed alongside thiamine in the lecture.
NUCLEIC ACIDSDNA and RNA are built on nitrogen-containing heterocyclic bases — the lecture cites nucleic acids directly as heterocyclic examples.
HAEMOGLOBIN / CHLOROPHYLLBoth rely on nitrogen-containing heterocyclic ring systems (porphyrins) at their core, and are listed by the lecture among the heterocyclic compounds fundamental to life.
Recall from the Classification tab: a heterocyclic ring contains more than one kind of atom — in addition to carbon, one or more of O, N or S may be present.
